claim: Executive function develops during adolescence.
source: Executive function develops during adolescence, yet it remains unknown how structural brain networks mature to facilitate activation of the fronto-parietal system, which is critical for executive function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: The fronto-parietal system is critical for executive function.
source: Executive function develops during adolescence, yet it remains unknown how structural brain networks mature to facilitate activation of the fronto-parietal system, which is critical for executive function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The study included 946 human youths aged 8-23 years who completed diffusion imaging.
source: In a sample of 946 human youths (ages 8-23y) who completed diffusion imaging, we capitalized upon recent advances in linear dynamical network control theory to calculate the energetic cost necessary to activate the fronto-parietal system through the control of multiple brain regions given existing structural network topology.
evidence: The sample size and age range are explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The energy required to activate the fronto-parietal system declined with development.
source: We found that the energy required to activate the fronto-parietal system declined with development, and the pattern of regional energetic cost predicts unseen individuals' brain maturity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses presented in the results.

claim: The pattern of regional energetic cost predicts unseen individuals' brain maturity.
source: We found that the energy required to activate the fronto-parietal system declined with development, and the pattern of regional energetic cost predicts unseen individuals' brain maturity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by machine learning analyses in the results.

claim: Energetic requirements of the cingulate cortex were negatively correlated with executive performance.
source: Finally, energetic requirements of the cingulate cortex were negatively correlated with executive performance, and partially mediated the development of executive performance with age.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analyses in the results.

claim: Energetic requirements of the cingulate cortex partially mediated the development of executive performance with age.
source: Finally, energetic requirements of the cingulate cortex were negatively correlated with executive performance, and partially mediated the development of executive performance with age.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mediation analyses in the results.

claim: Executive function is strongly associated with overall intelligence.
source: Executive function is essential for a wide range of cognitive tasks, and is strongly associated with both overall intelligence (Arffa, 2007) and academic performance (Best et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arffa, 2007.

claim: Executive function is strongly associated with academic performance.
source: Executive function is essential for a wide range of cognitive tasks, and is strongly associated with both overall intelligence (Arffa, 2007) and academic performance (Best et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Best et al., 2011.

claim: Executive function undergoes protracted maturation during adolescence.
source: Executive function undergoes protracted maturation during adolescence (Best and Miller, 2010; Gur et al., 2012), and its development is linked to the expansion of the cognitive and behavioral repertoire.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Best and Miller, 2010 and Gur et al., 2012.

claim: Executive deficits are linked to increased morbidity associated with risk-taking behaviors.
source: Notably, executive deficits are linked to both increased morbidity associated with risk-taking behaviors (Romer et al., 2009) as well as a wide range of neuropsychiatric disorders (Shanmugan et al., 2016), such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and psychosis (Barkley, 1997; Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Romer et al., 2009.

claim: Executive deficits are linked to a wide range of neuropsychiatric disorders such as ADHD and psychosis.
source: Notably, executive deficits are linked to both increased morbidity associated with risk-taking behaviors (Romer et al., 2009) as well as a wide range of neuropsychiatric disorders (Shanmugan et al., 2016), such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and psychosis (Barkley, 1997; Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shanmugan et al., 2016; Barkley, 1997; and Wolf et al., 2015.

claim: Executive function relies on activity in a distributed network of fronto-parietal regions, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex, superior parietal cortex, and frontopolar cortex.
source: Prior studies have consistently established that executive function relies on activity in a distributed network of fronto-parietal regions, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex, superior parietal cortex, and frontopolar cortex (Alvarez and Emory, 2006; Mansouri et al., 2017; Niendam et al., 2012; Rottschy et al., 2012; Satterthwaite et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Alvarez and Emory, 2006; Mansouri et al., 2017; Niendam et al., 2012; Rottschy et al., 2012; Satterthwaite et al., 2013.

claim: Functional connectivity among executive regions undergoes active remodeling during adolescence.
source: Notably, both functional (Fair et al., 2007; Grayson and Fair, 2017; Gu et al., 2015; Power et al., 2010) and structural (Baum et al., 2017; Hagmann et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015) connectivity among these regions undergoes active remodeling during adolescence, with increased connectivity among executive regions, and diminished connectivity between executive regions and other systems such as the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fair et al., 2007; Grayson and Fair, 2017; Gu et al., 2015; Power et al., 2010.

claim: Structural connectivity among executive regions undergoes active remodeling during adolescence.
source: Notably, both functional (Fair et al., 2007; Grayson and Fair, 2017; Gu et al., 2015; Power et al., 2010) and structural (Baum et al., 2017; Hagmann et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015) connectivity among these regions undergoes active remodeling during adolescence, with increased connectivity among executive regions, and diminished connectivity between executive regions and other systems such as the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baum et al., 2017; Hagmann et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015.

claim: Adolescence is characterized by increased connectivity among executive regions.
source: Notably, both functional (Fair et al., 2007; Grayson and Fair, 2017; Gu et al., 2015; Power et al., 2010) and structural (Baum et al., 2017; Hagmann et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015) connectivity among these regions undergoes active remodeling during adolescence, with increased connectivity among executive regions, and diminished connectivity between executive regions and other systems such as the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is supported by the same citations as the previous claims about connectivity remodeling.

claim: Adolescence is characterized by diminished connectivity between executive regions and other systems such as the default mode network.
source: Notably, both functional (Fair et al., 2007; Grayson and Fair, 2017; Gu et al., 2015; Power et al., 2010) and structural (Baum et al., 2017; Hagmann et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015) connectivity among these regions undergoes active remodeling during adolescence, with increased connectivity among executive regions, and diminished connectivity between executive regions and other systems such as the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is supported by the same citations as the previous claims about connectivity remodeling.

claim: Structural white matter networks constrain both intrinsic connectivity and patterns of task-related activation.
source: As structural white matter networks are known to constrain both intrinsic connectivity and patterns of task-related activation (Hermundstad et al., 2013; Honey et al., 2009), it is possible that white matter networks develop during adolescence to facilitate dynamic transitions to fronto-parietal system activation states with lower theoretical energetic cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hermundstad et al., 2013 and Honey et al., 2009.

claim: The brain becomes more theoretically controllable to all possible brain states through the control of individual brain regions during adolescence.
source: Previous work has shown that the brain becomes more theoretically controllable to all possible brain states (on average) through the control of individual brain regions during adolescence (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: The average energetic costs to reach the fronto-parietal activation target state varied by cognitive system, with the largest energetic costs being present in the fronto-parietal control network and the ventral attention network.
source: (b) The average energetic costs to reach the fronto-parietal activation target state varied by cognitive system, with the largest energetic costs being present in the fronto-parietal control network and the ventral attention network.
evidence: This claim is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1b and is supported by the data shown in the figure.

claim: The control energy cost of a transition to the fronto-parietal activation target state was significantly lower in real brain networks than in null model networks where the strength and degree distribution were preserved.
source: (d) The control energy cost of a transition to the fronto-parietal activation target state was significantly lower in real brain networks than in null model networks where the strength and degree distribution were preserved.
evidence: This claim is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1d and is supported by the data shown in the figure.

claim: The mean whole brain energetic cost of the null networks was significantly higher (p<2 × 10−16) than that of the empirical networks.
source: The mean whole brain energetic cost of the null networks was significantly higher (p<2 × 10−16) than that of the empirical networks (Figure 1d), indicating that structural brain networks are topologically optimized to reduce the energetic costs of the transition to a fronto-parietal activation state.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing empirical and null networks.

claim: Structural brain networks are topologically optimized to reduce the energetic costs of the transition to a fronto-parietal activation state.
source: The mean whole brain energetic cost of the null networks was significantly higher (p<2 × 10−16) than that of the empirical networks (Figure 1d), indicating that structural brain networks are topologically optimized to reduce the energetic costs of the transition to a fronto-parietal activation state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between empirical and null networks.

claim: The whole-brain average energetic cost of the transition to the fronto-parietal activation state declined with age (Z = −5.12, p=3.06 × 10−7, Partial r = −0.17, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [−0.23,–0.10]).
source: These analyses revealed that the whole-brain average energetic cost of the transition to the fronto-parietal activation state declined with age (Z = −5.12, p=3.06 × 10−7, Partial r = −0.17, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [−0.23,–0.10]; Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using generalized additive models.

claim: The largest declines in control energy with age occurred in fronto-parietal (Z = −5.30, PFDR = 4.54 × 10−7, Partial r = −0.17, CI = [−0.23,–0.11]), visual (Z = −4.25, PFDR = 5.71 × 10−5, Partial r = −0.14, CI = [−0.20,–0.08]), and motor (Z = −3.20, PFDR = 2.70 × 10−3, Partial r = −0.09, CI = [−0.15,–0.03]) systems.
source: Notably, analyses of cognitive systems indicated that age effects were heterogeneously distributed (Figure 2b), with the largest declines in control energy occurring in fronto-parietal (Z = −5.30, PFDR = 4.54 × 10−7, Partial r = −0.17, CI = [−0.23,–0.11]; Figure 2c), visual (Z = −4.25, PFDR = 5.71 × 10−5, Partial r = −0.14, CI = [−0.20,–0.08]), and motor (Z = −3.20, PFDR = 2.70 × 10−3, Partial r = −0.09, CI = [−0.15,–0.03]) systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of system-level control energy.

claim: Energetic costs within the limbic (Z = 8.69, PFDR <2 × 10−16, Partial r = 0.29, CI = [0.23, 0.35]) and default mode (Z = 2.86, PFDR = 5.66 × 10−3, Partial r = 0.10, CI = [0.04, 0.17]) systems increased with age.
source: In contrast, energetic costs within the limbic (Z = 8.69, PFDR <2 × 10−16, Partial r = 0.29, CI = [0.23, 0.35]) and default mode (Z = 2.86, PFDR = 5.66 × 10−3, Partial r = 0.10, CI = [0.04, 0.17]) systems increased with age (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of system-level control energy.

claim: The control energy of 49 regions decreased significantly with age (PFDR <0.05), including regions in the fronto-parietal control, visual, and motor systems.
source: These system-level results aligned with analyses of individual network nodes; we found that the control energy of 49 regions decreased significantly with age (PFDR <0.05), including regions in the fronto-parietal control, visual, and motor systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by nodal-level statistical analyses.

claim: The control energy significantly increased with development in 30 regions (PFDR <0.05), which were mainly situated in limbic and default mode systems.
source: Furthermore, the control energy significantly increased with development in 30 regions (PFDR <0.05), which were mainly situated in limbic and default mode systems (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by nodal-level statistical analyses.

claim: The multivariate pattern of control energy could predict an unseen individual's age with a correlation of 0.63 (p < 0.001) after controlling for covariates.
source: This analysis revealed that the multivariate pattern of control energy could predict an unseen individual's age (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b): the correlation between the predicted 'brain age' and chronological age was 0.63 (p < 0.001) after controlling for the covariates, and the mean absolute error (MAE) was 2.16 years (p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning prediction analyses with cross-validation.

claim: The mean absolute error (MAE) for predicting brain age from control energy was 2.16 years (p < 0.001).
source: This analysis revealed that the multivariate pattern of control energy could predict an unseen individual's age (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b): the correlation between the predicted 'brain age' and chronological age was 0.63 (p < 0.001) after controlling for the covariates, and the mean absolute error (MAE) was 2.16 years (p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning prediction analyses with cross-validation.

claim: The regions that contributed the most to the prediction of brain maturity included the dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, the cingulate cortex, superior parietal cortex, and lateral temporal cortex.
source: We further examined model weights at the level of individual network nodes. The regions that contributed the most to the prediction of brain maturity aligned with mass-univariate analyses, and included the dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, the cingulate cortex, superior parietal cortex, and lateral temporal cortex (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of model weights from the machine learning prediction model.

claim: Reduced control energy within the left middle cingulate cortex was associated with higher executive function (Z = −3.65, PFDR = 0.032, Partial r = −0.13, CI = [−0.19–0.06]).
source: Specifically, reduced control energy within two regions in the fronto-parietal control system -- the left and right middle cingulate cortex -- was associated with higher executive function (Left: Z = −3.65, PFDR = 0.032, Partial r = −0.13, CI = [−0.19–0.06]; Right: Z = −4.49, PFDR = 0.002, Partial r = −0.15, CI = [−0.21–0.08]; Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between control energy and executive function.

claim: Reduced control energy within the right middle cingulate cortex was associated with higher executive function (Z = −4.49, PFDR = 0.002, Partial r = −0.15, CI = [−0.21–0.08]).
source: Specifically, reduced control energy within two regions in the fronto-parietal control system -- the left and right middle cingulate cortex -- was associated with higher executive function (Left: Z = −3.65, PFDR = 0.032, Partial r = −0.13, CI = [−0.19–0.06]; Right: Z = −4.49, PFDR = 0.002, Partial r = −0.15, CI = [−0.21–0.08]; Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between control energy and executive function.

claim: Control energy in the left middle cingulate cortex (β = 0.03, p=0.001, 95% confidence interval = [0.01, 0.04]) mediated the development of executive function with age.
source: Using a bootstrapped mediation analysis while adjusting for the covariates described above (See Materials and methods), we found that control energy in both the left (β = 0.03, p=0.001, 95% confidence interval = [0.01, 0.04]; Figure 4c) and right middle cingulate cortex (β = 0.03, p<0.001, 95% confidence interval = [0.02, 0.05]; Figure 4d) mediated the development of executive function with age.
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrapped mediation analysis.

claim: Control energy in the right middle cingulate cortex (β = 0.03, p<0.001, 95% confidence interval = [0.02, 0.05]) mediated the development of executive function with age.
source: Using a bootstrapped mediation analysis while adjusting for the covariates described above (See Materials and methods), we found that control energy in both the left (β = 0.03, p=0.001, 95% confidence interval = [0.01, 0.04]; Figure 4c) and right middle cingulate cortex (β = 0.03, p<0.001, 95% confidence interval = [0.02, 0.05]; Figure 4d) mediated the development of executive function with age.
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrapped mediation analysis.

claim: 340 subjects were excluded owing to clinical factors, such as medical disorders.
source: Overall, 1601 participants were enrolled (Satterthwaite et al., 2014). However, 340 subjects were excluded owing to clinical factors including medical disorders that could affect brain function, current use of psychoactive medications, prior inpatient psychiatric treatment, or an incidentally encountered structural brain abnormality.
evidence: This is a description of the sample selection process.

claim: 54 subjects were excluded for a low quality T1-weighted image or errors in the FreeSurfer reconstruction.
source: Among the 1261 subjects eligible for inclusion, 54 subjects were excluded for a low quality T1-weighted image or errors in the FreeSurfer reconstruction.
evidence: This is a description of the sample selection process.

claim: 110 subjects failed quality assurance as part a rigorous quality assurance protocol for diffusion MRI.
source: Of the 1079 subjects with complete diffusion data, 110 subjects failed quality assurance as part a rigorous quality assurance protocol for diffusion MRI (Roalf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the sample selection process with citation to the QA protocol.

claim: The Penn computerized neurocognitive battery (Penn CNB) consists of 14 tests adapted from tasks applied in functional neuroimaging to evaluate a broad range of cognitive domains.
source: The Penn computerized neurocognitive battery (Penn CNB) was administered to all participants during a separate session from neuroimaging. The CNB consists of 14 tests adapted from tasks applied in functional neuroimaging to evaluate a broad range of cognitive domains (Gur et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the cognitive assessment method with citation.

claim: A factor analysis was used to summarize efficiency scores into four factors, including executive function, complex reasoning, memory, and social cognition.
source: A factor analysis was used to summarize these efficiency scores into four factors (Moore et al., 2015), including executive function, complex reasoning, memory, and social cognition.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method with citation.

claim: All MRI scans were acquired on the same 3T Siemens Tim Trio whole-body scanner and 32-channel head coil at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania.
source: As previously described (Satterthwaite et al., 2014), all MRI scans were acquired on the same 3T Siemens Tim Trio whole-body scanner and 32-channel head coil at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging acquisition parameters.

claim: Structural white matter networks were reconstructed for each participant from diffusion imaging data using probabilistic tractography and a standard parcellation of 232 regions.
source: Structural white matter networks were reconstructed for each participant from diffusion imaging data using probabilistic tractography and a standard parcellation of 232 regions.
evidence: This is a description of the network reconstruction method.

claim: The trajectory distance was inversely related to the time-dependent energy cost within subject.
source: Consistent with a recent methodological study (Karrer et al., 2019), and several recent empirical studies (Betzel et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2017; Stiso et al., 2019), the trajectory distance (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b) was inversely related to the time-dependent energy cost within subject (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological and empirical studies.

claim: The total trajectory distance of all time points was positively correlated with total control energy of all time points (r = 0.97, p<2 × 10−16).
source: Across all subjects, we found the total trajectory distance of all time points was positively correlated with total control energy of all time points (r = 0.97, p<2 × 10−16, Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), suggesting that subjects whose state transition trajectory is long require more energy input to reach the target state.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Control energy cost is lower in human brain than in the brains of Drosophila and mouse to support diverse network dynamics.
source: Prior literature has demonstrated that control energy cost is lower in human brain than in the brains of Drosophila and mouse to support diverse network dynamics (Kim et al., 2018), is related to network topology (Betzel et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2018) and reflects the magnitude of focal electrocorticography stimulation required to drive the brain to a target memory state in patients with medically refractory epilepsy (Stiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2018.

claim: Control energy is related to network topology.
source: Prior literature has demonstrated that control energy cost is lower in human brain than in the brains of Drosophila and mouse to support diverse network dynamics (Kim et al., 2018), is related to network topology (Betzel et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2018) and reflects the magnitude of focal electrocorticography stimulation required to drive the brain to a target memory state in patients with medically refractory epilepsy (Stiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Betzel et al., 2016 and Kim et al., 2018.

claim: Control energy reflects the magnitude of focal electrocorticography stimulation required to drive the brain to a target memory state in patients with medically refractory epilepsy.
source: Prior literature has demonstrated that control energy cost is lower in human brain than in the brains of Drosophila and mouse to support diverse network dynamics (Kim et al., 2018), is related to network topology (Betzel et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2018) and reflects the magnitude of focal electrocorticography stimulation required to drive the brain to a target memory state in patients with medically refractory epilepsy (Stiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stiso et al., 2019.

claim: While controlling for modal controllability, average control energy of the whole-brain and fronto-parietal system both significantly declined with age.
source: Specifically, while controlling for modal controllability, average control energy of the whole-brain and fronto-parietal system both significantly declined with age (whole-brain: Z = −6.00, p=2.09 × 10−9, Partial r = −0.19, CI = [−0.25,–0.13]; fronto-parietal: Z = −9.95, PFDR <2 × 10−16, Partial r = −0.32, CI = [−0.37,–0.26]).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis controlling for modal controllability.

claim: Results remained consistent after controlling for network modularity in all analyses.
source: Sixth, because the modularity of brain networks evolves with age, one could ask whether that evolution impacts the observed assocations with control energy (Baum et al., 2017; Hagmann et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2015). However, we found that results remained consistent after controlling for network modularity in all analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis controlling for network modularity.

claim: While controlling for within fronto-parietal connectivity strength, the control energy in the fronto-parietal system still significantly declined with development (Z = −3.53, p=0.0004, Partial r = −0.12, CI = [−0.18,–0.06]).
source: While controlling for within fronto-parietal connectivity strength, the control energy in the fronto-parietal system still significantly declined with development (Z = −3.53, p=0.0004, Partial r = −0.12, CI = [−0.18,–0.06]).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis controlling for connectivity strength.

claim: While controlling for the connectivity strength between the fronto-parietal system and other systems, the control energy in the fronto-parietal system still significantly declined with development (Z = −4.88, p=1.06 × 10−6, Partial r = −0.16, CI = [−0.22,–0.10]).
source: Similarly, while controlling for the connectivity strength between the fronto-parietal system and other systems, the control energy in the fronto-parietal system still significantly declined with development (Z = −4.88, p=1.06 × 10−6, Partial r = −0.16, CI = [−0.22,–0.10]).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis controlling for connectivity strength.

claim: Using an alternative target state defined by the average activation pattern elicited by an n-back working memory task, the control energy cost of the real network was significantly lower than null networks.
source: Using this alternative target state, we found that the control energy cost of the real network was significantly lower than null networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis using an alternative biologically-defined target state.

claim: Using an alternative target state from the n-back task, the whole-brain average control energy cost (Z = −7.59, p=3.26 × 10−14, Partial r = −0.25, CI = [−0.30,–0.18]) significantly declined with age.
source: Similarly, the whole-brain average control energy cost (Z = −7.59, p=3.26 × 10−14, Partial r = −0.25, CI = [−0.30,–0.18]; Figure 2—figure supplement 4d) and average control energy in the fronto-parietal system (Z = −5.26, PFDR = 2.92 × 10−7, Partial r = −0.17, CI = [−0.23,–0.11]; Figure 2—figure supplement 4e) both significantly declined with age.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis using an alternative biologically-defined target state.

claim: The middle cingulate is a component of the fronto-parietal control system and is critical for executive tasks such as performance monitoring, error detection, and task switching.
source: The middle cingulate is a component of the fronto-parietal control system (Fair et al., 2007; Yeo et al., 2011) and is critical for executive tasks such as performance monitoring, error detection, and task switching (Apps et al., 2013; Vogt, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fair et al., 2007; Yeo et al., 2011; Apps et al., 2013; and Vogt, 2016.

claim: Executive function training improves efficiency in activating the executive network.
source: This result is consistent with prior studies showing that executive function training improves efficiency in activating the executive network (Kozasa et al., 2012; Rueda et al., 2012), and that subjects with higher cognitive performance have lower brain cerebral metabolism cost in resting-state (Bastin et al., 2012) and have improved metabolic control (Ryan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kozasa et al., 2012 and Rueda et al., 2012.

claim: Subjects with higher cognitive performance have lower brain cerebral metabolism cost in resting-state.
source: This result is consistent with prior studies showing that executive function training improves efficiency in activating the executive network (Kozasa et al., 2012; Rueda et al., 2012), and that subjects with higher cognitive performance have lower brain cerebral metabolism cost in resting-state (Bastin et al., 2012) and have improved metabolic control (Ryan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bastin et al., 2012.

claim: Subjects with higher cognitive performance have improved metabolic control.
source: This result is consistent with prior studies showing that executive function training improves efficiency in activating the executive network (Kozasa et al., 2012; Rueda et al., 2012), and that subjects with higher cognitive performance have lower brain cerebral metabolism cost in resting-state (Bastin et al., 2012) and have improved metabolic control (Ryan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ryan et al., 2006.

claim: The decline of control energy cost reflects the optimization of the structural brain network.
source: This result is consistent with prior literature suggesting that the optimization of the structural network is associated with better executive function (Baum et al., 2017; Wen et al., 2011), as the decline of control energy cost reflects the optimization of the structural brain network (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baum et al., 2017; Wen et al., 2011; and Kim et al., 2018.

claim: The mediation effect of control energy on the relationship between age and executive function was small, as the direct effect was much larger than the indirect effect.
source: However, it should be noted that this mediation effect was small, as the direct effect was much larger than the indirect effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results.

claim: Linearization offers fundamental insights into nonlinear dynamics.
source: Nonetheless, it has been consistently demonstrated that linearization offers fundamental insights into nonlinear dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Predictions of function from structure can be obtained with both linear and nonlinear models.
source: For example, Honey et al. (2009) shows that predictions of function from structure can be obtained with both linear and nonlinear models.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Honey et al., 2009.

claim: If the linearized system is locally controllable along a specific trajectory in state space, then the original nonlinear system is also controllable along the same trajectory.
source: Second, if the linearized system is locally controllable along a specific trajectory in state space, then the original nonlinear system is also controllable along the same trajectory (Coron, 2007; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coron, 2007 and Yan et al., 2017.

claim: Linear controllers are often used to control nonlinear systems through gain scheduling in flight and process control.
source: Finally, linear controllers are often used to control nonlinear systems through gain scheduling in flight and process control (Leith and Leithead, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leith and Leithead, 2000.

claim: All data presented in the study were cross-sectional, which precludes inference regarding within-individual developmental effects.
source: First, all data presented here were cross-sectional, which precludes inference regarding within-individual developmental effects.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Probabilistic tractography methods remain limited in their ability to fully resolve the complex white matter architecture of the human brain.
source: Second, it should be noted that probabilistic tractography methods remain limited in their ability to fully resolve the complex white matter architecture of the human brain.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Probabilistic tractography may be superior to tensor-based tractography in resolving crossing fibers.
source: However, these methods are currently considered state-of-the-art, and may be superior to tensor-based tractography in resolving crossing fibers (Behrens et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Behrens et al., 2007.

claim: Motion artifact is a major potential confound for any study of brain development.
source: Third, it should be noted that motion artifact is a major potential confound for any study of brain development, and prior studies by our group and others have shown that motion artifact can bias estimates of tractography and confound developmental inference (Baum et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baum et al., 2018.

claim: Small samples systematically inflate the apparent effect size.
source: However, prior work has consistently demonstrated that small samples systematically inflate the apparent effect size (Yarkoni, 2009), whereas large samples (such as this one, n = 946) provide a much more accurate estimate of the true effect size.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yarkoni, 2009.

claim: Large samples provide a much more accurate estimate of the true effect size.
source: However, prior work has consistently demonstrated that small samples systematically inflate the apparent effect size (Yarkoni, 2009), whereas large samples (such as this one, n = 946) provide a much more accurate estimate of the true effect size.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Yarkoni, 2009.

claim: Motor development is largely complete by late childhood or early adolescence.
source: However, the non-significant developmental effect with motor target state is consistent with the evidence that motor development is largely complete by late childhood or early adolescence (Andersen, 2003; Gogtay et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andersen, 2003 and Gogtay et al., 2004.

claim: The topological structure of white matter networks is optimized during development to facilitate transitions to a fronto-parietal activation state.
source: These potential limitations notwithstanding, we demonstrated that the topological structure of white matter networks is optimized during development to facilitate transitions to a fronto-parietal activation state.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Structural brain networks exhibit non-random topological properties, such as both high clustering and segregated modules.
source: This result was consistent with prior studies showing that human structural brain networks exhibit non-random topological properties, such as both high clustering and segregated modules (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Gong et al., 2009b; Hagmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Gong et al., 2009b; and Hagmann et al., 2008.

claim: Metabolism costs declined in youth at both resting-state and during working memory tasks.
source: Consistent with our results, prior work has demonstrated that metabolism costs declined in youth at both resting-state (Jog et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 1999) and during working memory tasks (Jog et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jog et al., 2016 and Takahashi et al., 1999.

claim: The fronto-parietal system becomes more segregated in development from other systems in association cortex.
source: This result was consistent with previous studies using both structural and functional connectivity data, which have shown that the fronto-parietal system becomes more segregated in development from other systems in association cortex (Grayson and Fair, 2017; He et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2015; Lee and Telzer, 2016; Sherman et al., 2014), including the default mode (Sherman et al., 2014) and limbic (Lee and Telzer, 2016) systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grayson and Fair, 2017; He et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2015; Lee and Telzer, 2016; and Sherman et al., 2014.

claim: Modal controllability quantifies the general controllability necessary to reach all possible states.
source: However, modal controllability quantifies the general controllability necessary to reach all possible states, and therefore is not sufficient to answer questions about specific patterns of activity.
evidence: This is a description of what modal controllability measures.

claim: The whole brain control energy cost to activate the fronto-parietal system when constraining the whole brain was highly significantly correlated with the energy cost when only the fronto-parietal system was constrained (r = 0.94, p<2 × 10−16).
source: (d), The whole-brain control energy cost to activate the fronto-parietal system when constraining the whole brain was highly significantly correlated with the energy cost when only the fronto-parietal system was constrained (r = 0.94, p<2 × 10−16).
evidence: This claim is stated in the figure caption and supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The whole-brain control energy required to transition to the motor system activation did not significantly change over the age range studied (Z = 1.48, p=0.14, Partial r = 0.05, CI = [−0.02, 0.11]).
source: We found that the whole-brain control energy required to transition to the motor system activation did not significantly change over the age range studied (Z = 1.48, p=0.14, Partial r = 0.05, CI = [−0.02, 0.11]; Figure 2—figure supplement 2e right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using a motor system target state.
